questions.topic: HTML5 Core: Elements, Semantic Tags & Attributes
questions.question: What is the primary technical function of the `<!DOCTYPE html>` declaration at the beginning of an HTML document?
options: It connects the HTML file to a remote cloud database server
It instructs the web browser's rendering engine to parse and render the document in standard HTML5 mode rather than legacy 'quirks mode'
It imports external JavaScript libraries automatically
It encrypts the HTML source code so users cannot inspect it
questions.explanation: The `<!DOCTYPE html>` declaration is a document type instruction informing the browser's HTML parser that the document is written in modern HTML5. Without this declaration, browsers fall back into 'quirks mode', attempting to emulate 1990s Netscape/IE bugs and breaking modern CSS layouts.

why_wrong.0: HTML cannot connect directly to databases; database connectivity requires server-side languages.
why_wrong.2: JavaScript libraries are imported using the `<script>` tag, not the DOCTYPE declaration.
why_wrong.3: HTML source code is transmitted in plain text and cannot be encrypted by a DOCTYPE tag.

questions.source: IFT 203 Slide 3: Introduction to HTML and Web Page Structure; MDN Doctype

questions.question: In modern HTML5 web standards, what is the exact difference between the `<strong>` element and the `<b>` element?
options: `<b>` renders text in red color, while `<strong>` renders text in blue color
`<strong>` conveys semantic importance and urgency (which assistive screen readers emphasize with a changed tone of voice), whereas `<b>` is purely presentational styling with zero semantic meaning
`<strong>` can only be used inside tables, while `<b>` can only be used inside headings
There is no difference whatsoever; both are identical and `<b>` is preferred in HTML5
questions.explanation: In HTML5, `<strong>` represents strong semantic importance, seriousness, or urgency, prompting screen readers to alter pitch or volume to indicate emphasis. In contrast, `<b>` simply applies visual bold styling without conveying any added semantic weight to search engines or screen readers.

why_wrong.0: Neither tag alters font color by default; both render in bold black text unless styled with CSS.
why_wrong.2: Both tags can be used across any text context in an HTML document.
why_wrong.3: HTML5 explicitly distinguishes semantic tags from presentational tags, recommending `<strong>` over `<b>` whenever meaning is intended.

questions.question:
Consider the following HTML snippet: ```html

Item 3

Item 4
``` How will these four items be rendered visually on the browser screen?
options: All four items will be displayed horizontally on a single unbroken line
Each of the four items will be placed on its own separate line
`Item 1` and `Item 2` will appear side-by-side on the first line; `Item 3` will start on a new line; and `Item 4` will start on a third new line below `Item 3`
`Item 1`, `Item 2`, and `Item 3` will appear on the first line, and `Item 4` on the second line
questions.explanation:
`` is an inline element, so `Item 1` and `Item 2` sit side-by-side on the same line. `

` is a block-level element, which forces a line break before itself, taking the full width on the second line. Because `

` is a block element, the subsequent `Item 4` is forced to start on a new, third line below the paragraph.

why_wrong.0:
`

` is a block-level element and cannot sit on the same line as preceding or succeeding inline elements.

questions.question: Why is replacing nested generic `<div>` tags with semantic HTML5 elements (`<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<article>`, `<footer>`) considered a software engineering best practice? (Select ALL that apply)
options: It enables assistive technologies (screen readers) to provide keyboard shortcut landmarks for visually impaired users to skip directly to primary navigation or main content
It improves Search Engine Optimization (SEO) by allowing search web crawlers to accurately index key article text and discard peripheral boilerplate
It significantly improves code readability and maintainability for developer teams by making the document structure self-documenting
It makes the web page load 100 times faster because semantic tags do not use electricity
questions.explanation: Semantic HTML5 provides three massive benefits: (1) Accessibility for screen readers and assistive devices, (2) SEO advantages by highlighting content hierarchy for search engine crawlers, and (3) clean, self-documenting maintainability for development teams. The claim about electrical usage is nonsense.

why_wrong.3: Semantic tags are text tokens parsed by browsers; they have zero relation to electrical physics or 100x speed claims.

questions.source: IFT 203 Slide 3; MDN Semantic HTML Guide

questions.topic: HTML5 Core: Elements, Semantic Tags & Attributes
questions.question: What does `<!DOCTYPE html>` do, and where must it appear?
questions.answer: It informs the web browser that the document is written in modern HTML5, forcing the rendering engine to render in standards mode. It MUST appear on the very first line of the document before the `<html>` tag.
questions.explanation: Standard opening declaration required in all HTML5 documents.

questions.topic: HTML5 Core: Elements, Semantic Tags & Attributes
questions.question: Compare the `id` attribute and the `class` attribute in HTML.
questions.answer: `id` must be unique across the entire document (only ONE element can have that specific id). `class` can be reused on multiple elements to apply identical styles or JavaScript behaviors.
questions.explanation: Crucial rule: id = unique fingerprint, class = shared category.

questions.topic: HTML5 Core: Elements, Semantic Tags & Attributes
questions.question: What is the difference between `<sub>` and `<sup>`? Give practical examples.
questions.answer:
`<sub>` creates subscript text below the baseline (e.g., Chemical formulas: `H<sub>2</sub>O`).
`<sup>` creates superscript text above the baseline (e.g., Mathematical powers: `x<sup>2</sup>`).
questions.explanation: Text formatting tags covered in IFT 203 Slide 3.

questions.topic: HTML5 Core: Elements, Semantic Tags & Attributes
questions.question: What is Semantic HTML, and why is it preferred over `<div>` tags?
questions.answer: Using tags that describe the meaning of the content (e.g., `<article>`, `<nav>`, `<header>`) rather than generic containers. It makes pages accessible to screen readers, understandable to search engine crawlers, and easier to maintain.
questions.explanation: Foundational principle of modern web engineering.

questions.topic: HTML5 Core: Elements, Semantic Tags & Attributes
questions.question: Contrast the `<head>` element with the `<body>` element.
questions.answer:
`<head>` contains machine-readable metadata about the page (title, character encoding, viewport, external stylesheet links) that is NOT rendered in the main window.
`<body>` contains all visible content (text, images, tables, forms) displayed to the user.
questions.explanation: The two primary subdivisions of an HTML document.

questions.topic: HTML5 Core: Elements, Semantic Tags & Attributes
questions.question: What is the purpose of `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">`?
questions.answer: It informs mobile browsers to set the screen width of the viewport to the actual physical width of the device and sets the initial zoom level to 100%, enabling responsive mobile CSS rendering without auto-zooming out.
questions.explanation: Mandatory for all modern mobile-responsive web development.

case_studies.scenario:
A government agency's public scholarship portal is audited for accessibility. The auditor notes that the portal is written as a pure 'div-soup': ```html
Home Apply
2026 Nile University Scholarship
Applications open Monday...
© 2026 Ministry
``` Blind applicants using screen readers report that they cannot skip the repetitive header links and cannot find the scholarship announcement without listening to the entire page from top to bottom.

sub_questions.topic: HTML5 Core: Elements, Semantic Tags & Attributes
sub_questions.question: Which combination of Semantic HTML5 elements directly resolves the screen reader navigation barrier by establishing navigable landmark regions?
options: Replacing all `<div>` tags with `<span>` tags
Wrapping the top links in `<nav>`, the main announcement in `<main>` and `<article>`, the heading in `<h1>`, and the bottom in `<footer>`
Deleting all CSS styles from the server
Wrapping the entire page inside a `<marquee>` tag
sub_questions.explanation: Assistive screen readers allow users to press shortcut keys (e.g., 'H' for next heading, 'D' for next landmark) to jump directly between `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<article>`, and `<footer>` landmarks. Wrapping content in semantic landmarks allows blind students to immediately skip navigation and jump to the `<main>` article.

why_wrong.0: `<span>` is an inline element with zero semantic landmark capability.
why_wrong.2: Deleting CSS does not add structural landmarks to HTML markup.
why_wrong.3: `<marquee>` is an obsolete, non-standard tag that creates moving text and severely harms accessibility.

sub_questions.source: IFT 203 Slide 3; W3C Web Accessibility Initiative (WAI)

case_studies.scenario:
A student builds an online CV page for their take-home practical assignment. When viewed on a desktop computer, the page appears clean. However, when tested on a smartphone, two critical issues occur: (1) The text is microscopic because the mobile browser zooms out to fit a default 980px desktop canvas; (2) In the code, the student tried to insert multiple blank lines by typing multiple consecutive `
` tags and spaces inside a paragraph, but the browser collapses all whitespace into a single space.

sub_questions.topic: HTML5 Core: Elements, Semantic Tags & Attributes
sub_questions.question: What missing HTML element in the `<head>` causes the mobile browser to render the page in microscopic zoomed-out desktop canvas mode?
options: Missing `<!DOCTYPE html>`
`<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">`
`<meta charset="UTF-8">`
`<script src="jquery.js"></script>`
sub_questions.explanation: Mobile browsers default to a virtual 980px desktop viewport unless instructed otherwise. The `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">` tag tells the mobile browser to match the viewport width to the device's physical screen width and set the scale to 100%, making text readable without manual pinch-to-zoom.

why_wrong.0: Missing DOCTYPE triggers quirks mode, but does not control mobile device viewport scaling.
why_wrong.2: `<meta charset="UTF-8">` defines character encoding, not screen viewport scaling.
why_wrong.3: jQuery is a JavaScript library; viewport scaling is controlled natively by the HTML meta tag.

sub_questions.source: IFT 203 Slide 3; MDN Using the Viewport Meta Tag

sub_questions.topic: HTML5 Core: Elements, Semantic Tags & Attributes
sub_questions.question: Explain the HTML 'whitespace collapsing' rule that caused the student's spacing attempt to fail, and describe two correct ways to preserve formatted spacing or create vertical separation.
marking_points: Explains Whitespace Collapsing: HTML parsers collapse multiple consecutive spaces, tabs, and newline characters in source code into a single space during rendering.
Solution 1 (Preformatted Text): Using the `<pre>` tag, which renders text in a monospace font and preserves all consecutive spaces and line breaks exactly as typed.

Solution 2 (CSS Margins): Using CSS `margin-bottom` on paragraph elements rather than spamming multiple `
` tags, separating presentation from markup structure.
Notes non-breaking spaces ` ` as an inline character entity alternative.
sub_questions.answer:
1. Whitespace Collapsing Rule: Under standard W3C HTML parsing rules, any sequence of consecutive whitespace characters (including spaces, tabs, and newline line breaks) within text content is collapsed into a single space. Therefore, typing ten spaces or five blank lines in raw HTML code produces only a single space on screen. 2. Two Correct Solutions: - Solution 1: Use the `
` (Preformatted Text) Element: The `
` element instructs the browser engine to preserve every space, tab, and newline exactly as authored in the source file, rendered in a fixed-width monospace font. Ideal for poetry, ASCII art, or code snippets.
- Solution 2: Use CSS Margins for Vertical Spacing: Best practice dictates separating presentation from structure. Instead of hacking spacing with consecutive `


` tags, the developer should assign CSS margins (e.g., `margin-bottom: 2rem;`) to headings or paragraphs.
sub_questions.explanation: HTML collapses whitespace by design; preformatted text and CSS margins provide disciplined layout control.
